text: The top 10% of Americans now take home 46.8% of all pre-tax income, about the same share they had in 1929. In 1970 it was 33.5%.

Manhattan now has the most unequal incomes of any large county in America, and three of the top ten on this list from @[Steve Rattner](1658881) are in New York. Anyone who has walked from the Upper East Side into East Harlem has seen it within a few blocks.
why_now: Reshare: Rattner (Nov 19), Census Gini by county; Rattner reshares averaged a score of 59.

text: The top 0.1% of American households now hold 15% of all the wealth in the country, the highest share since the Fed started tracking it in 1989. Back then it was 8.6%.
why_now: Fed DFA Q2 2026 record; top-1% wealth note scored 100.

text: Wages and salaries now make up 42% of national income, tied for the lowest share since 1948. In the early 1950s it was above 51%.
Since 1984, GDP per person in America has doubled after inflation, while median household income is up 41%. Most of that growth went somewhere other than the typical family's paycheck.
In 1960, the top federal income tax rate in America was 91%. Today it's 37%.
why_now: Two-number format of the corporate-tax note (scored 89).

text:
The top 1% of Americans own 50.9% of all stocks. The bottom half of the country owns 0.6%.

I keep this in mind every time I see a headline about the stock market hitting another record.

72.5% of white households in America own their home, compared with 45.9% of Black households, per new Census data. Owning a home is still how most families build wealth, so this gap carries straight into the racial wealth gap.
After inflation, the price of a typical new home is up 68% since 1984, while median household income is up 41%. No wonder the typical first-time buyer is now 40.
why_now: Callback to the first-time buyer note (scored 91).

text: Since 2000, the dividend income Americans receive has grown 484%. Wages and salaries are up 185% over the same period. Most dividend income goes to the households with the biggest stock portfolios.
About 1 in 4 households in DC, Massachusetts and New Jersey now earn more than $200,000 a year. In Mississippi and West Virginia it's about 1 in 16.
why_now: ACS 2025; one map this week (maps were the weakest format).

text: Anthropic's 5,300 founders and employees are now worth about as much as the bottom third of US households combined, roughly 45 million families, in this chart from @[Steve Rattner](1658881).

text: The typical asking rent in America is now $1,913 a month, per Zillow. In October 2019 it was $1,369.
why_now: Single-number format of the first-time buyer note (scored 91).

text: Democrats' biggest gains in the midterms came in Texas and the Deep South, per this chart from @[Steve Rattner](1658881). I'd love to see how much of that shift came from voters worried about rent, groceries and health care.
